episode_title: Math is Better than the Brigadier's Girlfriend

stories.summary: During WWII, Allied intelligence wanted to know how many heavy tanks Germany was producing per month. Human-intelligence sources (the brigadiers' girlfriends) said roughly 1,500 a month. Statisticians took the serial numbers from sporadically captured/killed tanks, observed that the Germans assigned incremental numbers, and used the average inter-tank distance plus the highest observed serial to estimate the total. Their answer was roughly 200 a month. After the war, the German production records confirmed the statisticians were right and the spies were wrong.
stories.insight: A canonical demonstration that careful inference from a small, well-understood data structure can outperform a flood of human reports built on flattery and self-interest. Amit's punchline distills the politics of espionage: 'brigadiers lie to their girlfriends.'

stories.topic: Asking Dennis Aigner Whether Estimators Have a Limit
stories.summary: As a PhD student with no prior probability or statistics training, Ajay was placed in a fourth-year undergraduate econometrics class taught by Dennis Aigner. As Aigner walked through better and better estimators, Ajay raised his hand and asked whether there had to be a theoretical limit. Aigner replied that an Indian guy had asked the same question and got the answer — and that answer is the Cramér-Rao lower bound.
stories.insight: The right naive question, asked at the right moment, can lead you straight to one of the deepest results in a field. Beginner's mind is not a handicap — sometimes it's the path to the foundational question others stopped asking.

stories.topic: C.R. Rao at ISI: Two of the Greatest Theorems of 20th-Century Statistics
stories.summary: C.R. Rao, born in 1920 in South India, migrated to Calcutta and joined Mahalanobis's Indian Statistical Institute in the mid-40s — pre-independence, with no government money, run on Mahalanobis's personal funds. As a young man cut off from the European mainstream, Rao independently produced two of the great statistical results of the 20th century: the Cramer-Rao lower bound (the theoretical limit on how good an estimator can be) and the Rao-Blackwell theorem (a procedure for one-step improvement of estimators). Both were named jointly with Western co-discoverers because Ronald Fisher, with characteristic decency, recognised the work and started calling them by their joint names.
stories.insight: Greatness can emerge from an isolated outpost if you have one obsessive institution-builder around whom an ecosystem coheres. And recognition is not automatic — it required Fisher's personal generosity for Rao's work to enter the global canon, just as Darwin and Wallace shared credit because the Royal Society chose to honour both.

stories.topic: Ramanujan vs Anand: Two Models of Indian Genius
stories.summary: Ramanujan was completely self-taught from one obscure 19th-century textbook, then transported to Cambridge where G.H. Hardy translated his raw genius into world-class mathematics — the achievement was Cambridge's. Anand, by contrast, was largely built by an Indian ecosystem that nurtured and funded him; he then helped seed the next generation, who today are the strongest teen chess cohort in the world. Ajay places C.R. Rao on the Anand axis: not a precocious child shipped abroad, but a regular student who walked into Mahalanobis's ISI and exploded inside the ecosystem it provided.
stories.insight: Individual genius is one phenomenon; an ecosystem that cultivates many talents over decades is another, and they should not be confused. India can occasionally produce a Ramanujan; what it must learn to build are the Mahalanobis-style ecosystems that transform regular students into world-changing minds.

stories.summary: Ajay's collaborator Sourish Das, building a Bayesian-first statistical modelling package in Julia, came to him on a Monday and said he wanted to call it CRRao.jl as a commitment device — naming it after the legend would force them to do the work right. Later they got an email from Rao's daughter saying she had shown him the package and he had smiled. That smile, Ajay says, was the closest he ever came to the greatness of C.R. Rao.
stories.insight: A reminder that names function as constraints. Honouring a hero in code (or anywhere) is a public promise to live up to the standard the name implies. The hero's smile, in turn, is a quiet completion of a circle that crossed seventy years.

stories.topic: Why Indian Statistics Missed the Computational Revolution
stories.summary: Through the 1940s and 50s, Indian mathematical statistics — Mahalanobis, Rao and their generation — was at the global frontier of theorem-proving and closed-form estimators. In 1979 Bradley Efron developed the bootstrap, and the field shifted: the unit of analysis stopped being a closed-form mathematical estimator and became an algorithm. The Indian statistics community stayed wedded to the old style, kept proving theorems, and largely missed the data-science revolution that grew out of computational statistics.
stories.insight: Past excellence is not future excellence. Research communities, like artists, can be frozen at their hit moment. India was at the global frontier in mathematical statistics; staying there meant being late to the field that mathematical statistics gave birth to.

stories.topic: Abraham Wald and the Missing Bullet Holes
stories.summary: Around 1942, Abraham Wald was drafted into the Statistical Research Group — a body so brilliant that Milton Friedman was once described as the fourth smartest person in the room. Wald lacked security clearance, so a secretary stood by his side and whisked away each finished sheet of paper before he saw the next problem. Asked to advise where to add armour to British planes returning with bullet holes, the obvious answer was 'reinforce the fuselage' since that's where the holes were. Wald reframed it: where are the missing bullets? They are in the planes that did not return. Armour the engines — the part with no holes — because hits there are the ones that bring planes down.
stories.insight: The classic worked example of survivorship bias. The planes you see are the survivors; the data you don't have is the most important data. Always ask what is missing from the sample before you act on what is present.

stories.topic: Ricky Ponting Had a Map of the Gaps
stories.summary: Asked about his journey to greatness, Ricky Ponting said most batsmen carry a map of the fielders in their heads. He carried a map of the gaps.
stories.insight: Same Wald move in another domain: stop looking at where the obstacles are and look at where they aren't. Inverting the question is often the whole insight.

stories.topic: The Cricket-Tipster Scam as Survivorship Bias
stories.summary: Write to a thousand cricket bettors saying you can predict the result of the next India-Sri Lanka match. Tell five hundred India will win, five hundred Sri Lanka. Repeat with the surviving five hundred, then the surviving 250, then 125, until ten or twelve people have seen you correctly call six matches in a row. They will pay you handsomely. They are seeing only the surviving prediction strand; the 988 wrong calls are invisible to them. The same logic explains why a five- or six-year track record of a single mutual fund is meaningless when you can look back across a fund family.
stories.insight: Every 'amazing track record' raises the same question: out of how many starting attempts? Without the denominator, you cannot tell skill from selection.

stories.topic: How Many Lives Does It Take to Kill a Factory?
stories.summary: WWII bombers were so imprecise (circular error probability of 1-5 km) that bombing a tank factory or oil refinery from 20,000 feet meant throwing thousands of bombs and rarely hitting. Flying low at 6,000 feet improved precision dramatically but exposed crews to anti-aircraft 88mm flak. The young Robert McNamara and Curtis LeMay, working as quantitative thinkers, computed factories killed per pilot lost — and concluded that flying at 6,000 feet was the right answer. They told the pilots: 'We love you more than life itself, but the efficient way is to count how many of you die per unit factory.'
stories.insight: A brutal but honest example of utilitarian calculation in war. The cost is real and the language sounds monstrous, but refusing to do the math doesn't make the trade-off go away — it just hides it from the people making the decision.

stories.topic: Mahalanobis vs the Bengal Government on Counting Jute
stories.summary: In 1944 the Bengal government, sceptical of Mahalanobis's new random sample survey method, ran a competition: traditional plot-to-plot enumeration against the institute's sample survey, both compared against official jute sales figures. The cumbersome enumeration was off by 16.6%; the sample survey was off by only 0.3% — and cost a tenth as much. It was a moment of vindication for Mahalanobis and ISI.
stories.insight: Sometimes a clean head-to-head bake-off is the only thing that breaks an entrenched method. The savings here weren't marginal — better answers at one-tenth the cost. When the better tool is also the cheaper tool, the only reason for inertia is institutional ego.

stories.topic: Mahalanobis the Polymath and the Authoritarian
stories.summary: Drawing on Nikhil Menon's Planning Democracy, Amit paints a portrait of P.C. Mahalanobis — physicist by training, statistician by intellect, planner by conviction — Sanskrit reader, Bengali poetry connoisseur, dabbler in architecture, prim workaholic with hair slicked flat by coconut oil. Hannah Arendt described him as immensely vigorous, alert, and intelligent, but also domineering, vain, bigoted, and a Bengali aristocrat moving toward Stalinist authoritarianism. He required students and staff to record their daily activities in a diary and sign in and out of the institute. Milton Friedman warned that able mathematicians, working in a field of absolutes, become dangerous when they apply themselves to economic planning.
stories.insight: The same temperament that built ISI — the obsessive, controlling, certainty-seeking mind — turned ruinous when applied to the messy, complex, adaptive system of an economy. High modernism builds great institutions and broken economies, sometimes by the same person.

stories.topic: The Bharat Sadhu Samaj — When the State Tried to License Sadhus
stories.summary: In 1956 the Indian government, alarmed that there were an estimated 75 lakh sadhus and many were said to be frauds, brought a sadhu registration bill. The idea was that to be known as a sadhu you would apply to the government, get a license, and join the Bharat Sadhu Samaj. Once it was set up, President Rajendra Prasad addressed the licensed sadhus and told them their scriptures did not enjoin indifference to this world — and that supporting the five-year plan was the path to good in the next world.
stories.insight: An almost-comic distillation of high modernism's ambition: not just the economy, but spiritual practice itself, brought under state licensing in service of central planning. The fact that today's sadhus are not certified is its own quiet verdict.

stories.topic: J.B.S. Haldane Came to India Because He Didn't Want to Wear Socks
stories.summary: J.B.S. Haldane, the British polymath, moved to India in his 60s to work at ISI under Mahalanobis. Asked why he had left England, he didn't deliver a grand statement about simple living or freedom from convention. He said: 'I don't want to wear socks.' Photos from his Indian years show him in banyan, dhoti, pajama — never a sock in sight. (Of Mahalanobis's constant travel he wrote: 'The journeyings of our director define a novel random vector.')
stories.insight: A textbook 'show, don't tell' moment. The casual, bodily image — no socks — communicates an entire philosophy of life more vividly than any abstract phrase about freedom or simplicity could.

stories.topic: Abraham Wald Died in an Air India Crash After Speaking at ISI
stories.summary: After the Wald story comes a small, full-circle coda: Wald died in 1950 in an Air India plane crash, aged 48, with his wife. He had just given a talk at ISI in Calcutta and was on his way to the Indian Statistical Congress in Bangalore. So Milton Friedman, instead of being the fourth smartest in the room, became the third smartest — but not in a way he would have liked.
stories.insight: Tragic punctuation to a story about survivorship bias: the man who taught the world to look for the missing planes was himself one of them.

stories.topic: Chintaman Deshmukh Saved ISI and Married a Tree-Inscribed Proposal
stories.summary: Around 1944 Chintaman Deshmukh — later India's first Indian RBI Governor and Finance Minister — approved a flow of funds to ISI that practically guaranteed its survival. Nikhil Menon describes him as a diminutive, suave, cerebral product of elite Bombay and Cambridge education who topped the ICS, recited Vedic shlokas for pleasure, translated Kalidasa's Meghadūta from Sanskrit, and quoted scripture in economic policy. Widowed in the early 50s, he later married Durgabai Deshmukh — herself a remarkable woman who had walked out of her own child marriage at fourteen. The opening lines of her autobiography Chintaman and I: 'Chintaman took me to a eucalyptus tree in his garden and inscribed two Sanskrit shlokas on its bark. It was a proposal of marriage. I accepted, and he kissed me.'
stories.insight: A sketch of a vanished kind of public servant — scholar, polyglot, Sanskrit lover, and quietly romantic. As Amit notes: even people who care about statistics and math have hearts.

recommendations.creator: Shane Parrish (Farnam Street)
recommendations.context: A three-volume set from Farnam Street covering general thinking models, then physics and chemistry, then mathematics.
recommendations.reason: Formal education rarely teaches us how to think. These books supply the tools — frames, models, analogies — that let you find the commonalities between fields, the literal practice of 'everything is everything.' Gifted to Amit by his friend Gautam John; he says the Kindle copies are cheap and everyone should own them.

recommendations.creator: David Salsburg
recommendations.context: A history of how 20th-century statistics took shape, anchored in the famous Fisher experiment of testing whether a lady could really tell whether milk had been poured into tea or tea into milk.
recommendations.reason: Even if you have never done statistics, this book is fun. It uses concrete questions like the lady's tea claim to develop the ideas of testing, blind testing, and the mathematics behind them — the human and historical entry point into the field.

recommendations.creator: Nikhil Menon
recommendations.context: A history of the Planning Commission, P.C. Mahalanobis, and how data was gathered and used in the early Indian state.
recommendations.reason: The source of much of the Mahalanobis material in this episode — the jute survey vindication, the diary-and-attendance authoritarianism, the Bharat Sadhu Samaj, Chintaman Deshmukh. Essential for understanding the Nehruvian planning era from the inside.

recommendations.creator: Samanth Subramanian
recommendations.context: A biography of J.B.S. Haldane, the British polymath who moved to India and worked at ISI.
recommendations.reason: A beautifully written biography of a wild, eccentric genius who loved India enough to take Indian citizenship and refuse to wear socks. Captures both the spirit of mid-century scientific inquiry and the political radicalism of the man.

recommendations.creator: Durgabai Deshmukh
recommendations.context: Durgabai Deshmukh's autobiography, which opens with Chintaman Deshmukh's eucalyptus-tree marriage proposal in Sanskrit.
recommendations.reason: Out of print on Kindle and hard to find anywhere; Amit located a free copy on the internet and links it from the show notes. A first-person window into a remarkable woman who walked out of a child marriage at fourteen and later married one of independent India's most cultured public servants.

recommendations.creator: Jeff Bezanson, Stefan Karpinski, Viral Shah, Alan Edelman
recommendations.context: A modern programming language for high-performance scientific computing, co-created by Ajay's friend Viral Shah.
recommendations.reason: Solves the 'two language problem' — clean and understandable like Python, fast like C. Ajay considers it one of the great achievements of modern programming and the right substrate for the next generation of statistics and data science.

recommendations.creator: Sourish Das, XKDR Forum, Chennai Mathematical Institute
recommendations.context: An open-source Julia statistical modelling package providing a single uniform API across linear regression, Bayesian regression, random forests, and many other estimators — Bayesian by default, with no extra distance to cross.
recommendations.reason: Named after C.R. Rao as a commitment device to do the work right. Ajay believes a uniform Bayesian-first calling convention is what serious data science needs, and that Julia is the right substrate for it.

recommendations.reason: Listed as a useful resource. Amit's course on clear writing for anyone who wants to write more crisply.

core_ideas.explanation: An impossibility result for statistics: given a model and a data set, there is a theoretical floor on how good any unbiased estimator can be. You can keep designing better estimators, but you cannot cross the Cramer-Rao bound. C.R. Rao proved it in 1943 in Calcutta as a young man, independently of Cramer in Sweden. The reason this matters beyond statistics: it is one of the rare results that tells you not just what works but what cannot be beaten — a bound on what any future cleverness can achieve.
core_ideas.quote: There will be a theoretical limit on how good an estimator can get.

core_ideas.explanation: A constructive companion to the Cramer-Rao bound: a procedure that takes any estimator and produces a new one that is at least as good (and usually better) by conditioning on a sufficient statistic. It is the operational machinery for moving an estimator step by step toward the Cramer-Rao floor.

When you analyse a data set, you are usually analysing the survivors. The bombers in the hangar are the ones that didn't get hit in fatal places; the mutual funds with five-year records are the ones that didn't get killed; the cricket tipster who got six picks right is the one whose strand of forecasts didn't die. The most important data is often the data you do not see. Always ask, before acting on what is present, what is missing from this sample.

core_ideas.concept: From Closed-Form Estimators to Algorithms (Computational Statistics)
core_ideas.explanation: Until the 1970s, statistics meant proving theorems and writing estimators in closed mathematical form. Bradley Efron's 1979 invention of the bootstrap was part of a shift in which an estimator could be defined as an algorithm — a recipe a computer could carry out — rather than as a formula. This fused statistics with computer science and gave rise to modern data science. India's statistics community, anchored in the older theorem-proving tradition, was slow to make the jump.
core_ideas.quote: The unit of analysis stops being a mathematical estimator that can be written down in closed form, but the estimator becomes an algorithm.

core_ideas.concept: Ramanujan vs Anand: Two Models of Indian Talent
core_ideas.explanation: Ramanujan represents the lone, self-taught genius rescued and shaped by an external ecosystem (Cambridge, Hardy). His translation into greatness was the achievement of someone else's institution. Anand represents the genius produced and amplified by a domestic ecosystem — flawed but sufficient — who in turn helps build the next generation. India can occasionally accident a Ramanujan; sustained world-class output requires the patient construction of Anand-style ecosystems.

core_ideas.concept: The Mahalanobis Phenomenon: Eccentric Founders Beat Bureaucracies
core_ideas.explanation: ISI in the 1940s was world-class without government money — a private institution bootstrapped by one obsessive, confident, idiosyncratic person who attracted Fisher, Haldane, and others to Calcutta. Modern Indian public-sector research and education organisations, despite vastly more resources, have struggled to recreate that excellence. Ajay's reading: don't ask for more public-sector institutions; ask for more eccentric, confident, crazy, creative individuals empowered to build isolated centres of excellence.
core_ideas.quote: What you need is a Mahalanobis. What you don't need is a government bureaucracy.

core_ideas.explanation: The two-part conviction that scientists and engineers know what to do, and that their special claim on truth licenses them to coerce everyone else into following. It works in narrow control systems — one mathematical model, one piece of software — and breaks badly in the social world, where unknowability is the dominant feature. Mahalanobis the brilliant physicist became Mahalanobis the dangerous central planner because the certainty trained by physics did not survive contact with an economy. The 20th century is, in large part, a record of high modernism's failures.
core_ideas.quote: If there is one great thing we have learned through the twentieth century, it is that high modernism works pretty badly.

core_ideas.concept: Fisher's Decency and the Naming of Theorems
core_ideas.explanation: Indian work — even great work — has historically been brushed aside by the global mainstream, especially before the internet. Rao's 1943 results could easily have remained invisible. They didn't because Ronald Fisher, who occasionally visited ISI, recognised what was happening and chose to call them the Cramer-Rao lower bound and the Rao-Blackwell theorem. The same generosity, exercised by the Royal Society, gave Wallace co-credit with Darwin for natural selection. Naming is a moral act: who gets included in a theorem's title is a decision about what a discipline remembers.

Mahalanobis's 1944 jute experiment in Bengal showed that a well-designed random sample survey could be off by 0.3% (versus 16.6% for traditional plot-to-plot enumeration) at one-tenth the cost. The deeper point is that asking the right small question of a small sample, with proper inference, can dominate exhaustive counting — and can do so on both accuracy and price simultaneously.

A core writing principle: don't state your point in abstract words; show it through a concrete image or detail and let the reader infer. Haldane's answer to why he moved to India — 'I don't want to wear socks' — is a textbook instance. The vibe is immediate; nothing needs explaining; an entire ethic of life is conveyed without an adjective.

WWII bomber command's painful arithmetic: at 20,000 feet you survive but rarely hit the target; at 6,000 feet you hit more often but die more often. The decision is not 'which altitude feels less terrifying' but 'which altitude minimises pilots killed per factory destroyed.' Pricing in the cost of human lives explicitly, in the same units as the objective, is the unsentimental core of operations research — and a forerunner of how McNamara would later think about Vietnam.
core_ideas.quote: We love you more than life itself, but we want the efficient way to do it.

core_ideas.explanation: Sourish Das called the package CRRao.jl as a commitment device — naming it after the giant publicly bound the team to do the work to a standard worthy of the name. The mechanism generalises: name a thing after a hero, and you make it harder to deliver something shoddy. Reputation, even by association, is a form of constraint.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's punchline to the German Tank Problem: 'The moral of the story is — brigadiers lie to their girlfriends.'
Ajay on the Statistical Research Group: it was so brilliant that 'someone quipped Milton Friedman is the fourth smartest person in the room. Can you imagine?'
Amit closes the Wald story with Air India: after the 1950 crash, 'Milton Friedman would now be the third smartest man in the room — but not in a way he would have liked.'
Ajay on the standard sources of human intelligence in WWII: 'You have a spotter plane, you have local intelligence, you have the brigadier's girlfriend.'

Amit on Mahalanobis: after reading Nikhil Menon's portrait of a stern, prim, expression-withholding workaholic affectionate only to dogs, cats and cows, Amit turns to Ajay: 'I know not of your fondness for dogs and cows, but the rest of this seems to fit you.'
Amit on the cats fighting in the background mid-episode: 'That is a ghost of statisticians past who have worked at the ISI wailing to see the condition.'

Amit on Haldane's 'I don't want to wear socks' as a life-philosophy statement: 'Nobody likes wearing socks. I mean, unless they're kinda kinky and you know they wear it on their heads while doing unspeakable things — look up autoerotic asphyxiation.'

Amit on the Sadhu Samaj: 'Once the Bharat Sadhu Samaj was farmed — uh, formed; not farmed, you could farm them — with licensed and certificated sadhus, with the documentation in triplicate and all of that...'
Ajay riffing off the name CRRao.jl: 'We should have called the show CR. Everything is CR.' Amit: 'You would also have put more effort into what kind of shirt you're wearing — untucked and all that.'
Amit, after Ajay raises the lethal British-bomber dilemma over the German tank problem: 'You raised me, so I will just fold. I don't want to play the next hand I'm forced to play.'
Amit punning off Julia: 'As another Julia would say, the hills are alive with the sound of coding.'

Ajay claiming Bengal's catchment is unbounded: of South Indian C.R. Rao becoming 'the greatest achievement of the Bengali Renaissance' — 'we will certainly claim him as one of our own if you give us a chance.' Amit replies: 'All Bengali geniuses are belong to me, Dada.'

'Coming back on a wing and a prayer' — Ajay notes the phrase originated from WWII British and American bombers literally limping back to England with engines shot out, gliding home and praying to make it. One of the most beautiful phrases in the English language with a very specific factual origin.
Ricky Ponting's frame for batting greatness: 'Most batsmen have a map of the fielders in their head. I had a map of the gaps.'

Hannah Arendt on Mahalanobis (quoted by Amit): 'Immensely vigorous, alert and intelligent, but also domineering, vain and bigoted, a Bengali aristocrat who in moving towards Stalinist type authoritarianism has completely bypassed democratic liberal notions.'

Milton Friedman's warning about mathematicians as planners: 'Able mathematicians, working in a field of absolutes, tend to be dangerous when they apply themselves to economic planning. They produce specific and detailed plans in which they have confidence without realising that economic planning is not the absolute science that mathematics is.'
J.B.S. Haldane on Mahalanobis's restless travel: 'The journeyings of our director define a novel random vector.'

Durgabai Deshmukh's opening lines in Chintaman and I: 'Chintaman took me to a eucalyptus tree in his garden and inscribed two Sanskrit shlokas on its bark. It was a proposal of marriage. I accepted, and he kissed me.'

Darwin and Wallace in the Royal Society — the precedent Ajay invokes for joint credit: when Wallace's letter arrived after a malarial fever-dream insight, the Royal Society knew Darwin had been nursing the theory for twenty-five years and chose to present them together rather than let one displace the other.
Sankhya — the journal built out of ISI in its world-class era, respected globally and stocked by libraries everywhere. Cited as evidence of how high India's statistical institutions once flew.
